\chapter{Having and Telling Your Age}
\label{ch:pt-having-and-age}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask a Portuguese speaker's age and give my own, holding my years with ter rather than being them.}

Ask Quantos anos tens?, answer Tenho vinte anos — literally I hold twenty years — and set Portuguese's simplified ano against Spanish's palatalised año.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ter]{ter — \textquotedblleft{}to have\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C14-ter}



\begin{quote}
Every Romance language needs a word for \textquotedblleft{}have.\textquotedblright{} French and Italian took one from Latin; \textbf{Portuguese and Spanish took a different one entirely} — and it didn't originally mean \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{} at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
(eu) & \textbf{tenho} \\
(tu) & \textbf{tens} \\
(ele/ela/você) & \textbf{tem} \\
(nós) & \textbf{temos} \\
(vocês/eles) & \textbf{têm} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two things to watch:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{tenho} — the \textbf{-nh-} (Portuguese's palatal \emph{ny}, = Spanish \textbf{ñ}), already met in \emph{vinho} (Ch. 11) and \emph{amanhã}.
  \item \textbf{tem} vs \textbf{têm} — \textquotedblleft{}he has\textquotedblright{} vs \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{they} have\textquotedblright{}. They sound nearly alike; the \textbf{circumflex} marks the plural. An accent doing grammar, not sound.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ter} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{tenēre}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to hold}\textquotedblright{} — not \textquotedblleft{}to have.\textquotedblright{}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}to have\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{$\leftarrow$ Latin} \\
\midrule
French & \emph{avoir} & \emph{habēre} \\
Italian & \emph{avere} & \emph{habēre} \\
\textbf{Portuguese} & \textbf{ter} & \emph{\textbf{tenēre}} \textquotedblleft{}to hold\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{tener} & \emph{\textbf{tenēre}} \textquotedblleft{}to hold\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Portuguese \emph{does} still have \textbf{haver} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{habēre}) — but it got demoted to an auxiliary and to \emph{há} (\textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{}). So on the Iberian peninsula the two verbs \textbf{swapped jobs}: \textquotedblleft{}hold\textquotedblright{} moved up to mean \emph{have}, and \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{} moved down to a grammar word.

English kept the \emph{tenēre} family as borrowings: \textbf{tenant} (one who \emph{holds} land), \textbf{retain}, \textbf{maintain}, \textbf{tenacious}, \textbf{tenure}, \textbf{contain}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tenho, tens, tem, temos, têm\textquotedblright{}
  \item the \textbf{-nh-} — \textquotedblleft{}te\textbf{nh}o\textquotedblright{}, like \emph{vi\textbf{nh}o}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tenho um irmão\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}I have a brother\textquotedblright{}) — Ch. 10's family
  \item the hold-family — \textquotedblleft{}ter · tenant · retain · tenacious\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{ter}'s Latin source mean? (\emph{\textbf{Tenēre}} — \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{hold}\textquotedblright{}.) Which other language made the same swap? (\textbf{Spanish}, \emph{tener}.) What happened to Portuguese's \emph{habēre} verb? (It became \textbf{haver} — an auxiliary, and \emph{há} \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{}.) What separates \emph{tem} from \emph{têm}? (The \textbf{circumflex} — singular vs plural.) Next: the question \emph{ter} is used for that English would never use \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{} for.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tenho vinte anos]{tenho vinte anos — holding your years}

\label{lesson:PT-C14-idade}



\begin{quote}
Portuguese states age with \textbf{ter}. And since \emph{ter} came from \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{hold},\textquotedblright{} the sentence is, at the root, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I hold twenty years}\textquotedblright{} — the most physical version of this idea in any of the five languages.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The phrase}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quantos anos tens?} — \textquotedblleft{}How many years do you \textbf{have}?\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Tenho vinte anos.} — \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{have} twenty years.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ser} is wrong here. And \textbf{anos} can't be dropped, unlike English \textquotedblleft{}I'm twenty.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ano} (\textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{annus}} $\to$ English \textbf{annual}, \textbf{anniversary}, \textbf{annals}.

Now compare the two Iberian sisters:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{Portuguese} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
\emph{annus} & \textbf{ano} & \textbf{año} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The Latin \textbf{-nn-} went two ways: Portuguese \textbf{simplified} it to a plain \emph{n}, Spanish \textbf{palatalized} it into \textbf{ñ}. Same word, same peninsula, two outcomes — and this is exactly where Spanish's \emph{ñ} came from in the first place: doubled Latin \emph{n}.

Careful: keep \emph{ano} distinct from \emph{ânus}. The stress and the circumflex do the work.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Who has, who is}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
Portuguese & \emph{t\textbf{enho} vinte anos} & I \textbf{hold} … \\
Spanish & \emph{t\textbf{engo} veinte años} & I \textbf{hold} … \\
French & \emph{j'\textbf{ai} vingt ans} & I \textbf{have} … \\
Italian & \emph{h\textbf{o} venti anni} & I \textbf{have} … \\
German & \emph{ich \textbf{bin} zwanzig Jahre alt} & I \textbf{am} … \\
English & \emph{I \textbf{am} twenty} & I \textbf{am} … \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three layers: Germanic \textbf{is} its years, French and Italian \textbf{have} them, and Iberian Romance \textbf{holds} them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Quantos anos tens?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tenho vinte anos\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own age, using Ch. 12's numbers
  \item the sister pair — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ano} … \textbf{año}\textquotedblright{} — one Latin \emph{annus}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb does Portuguese use for age? (\emph{\textbf{Ter}}, never \emph{ser}.) Given \emph{ter}'s root, what does the sentence literally say? (\textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{hold} twenty years.\textquotedblright{}) Where does \emph{ano} come from? (Latin \emph{\textbf{annus}}.) What did Portuguese and Spanish each do with the \textbf{-nn-}? (PT \textbf{simplified} it to \emph{n}; ES \textbf{palatalized} it to \textbf{ñ}.) Which two languages say \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{am}\textquotedblright{} instead? (\textbf{German and English}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
